No, that isn't right, and it matters for your design. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own.

The model only sees the text it is sent in each call. Between calls it keeps nothing. Chatbots seem to remember because the app resends the whole conversation every time. Your homework chatbot "knows" what you said ten messages ago because that text is pasted into the prompt again. Start a new chat and it is gone.

Here is what that means for the makerspace assistant. Suppose Sam tells it on Monday, "I finished the laser cutter training." On the next Monday, Sam opens a new session. The model has no idea who Sam is or what Sam said. If you want it to know, your program has to do three things:

1. Save the fact somewhere, such as a file or a database row, when Sam says it.
2. Look it up at the start of the next session.
3. Put it into the prompt, for example "Sam completed laser cutter training on Nov 3."

So the memory lives in your program, and the model only sees what you hand it. This is the "what it saves between sessions" decision in your mission. It also touches your budget, because everything you put back into the prompt costs tokens on every call.

Your assistant can still remember each student, but you have to build that part yourself.

Quick check: in the Sam example, which part of the system does the remembering, and where would the "laser cutter training" fact live in the week between sessions?

If you want to go deeper, I can write a 15-minute lesson on context and memory. It's the next topic in your mission, and it covers what to save, what to reload, and what it costs.
